Memory

ArithmeticMental MathCounting
Game: Twenty cards lie face down. Turn two at a time and find the pairs that match, using as few turns as you can.
How to play: Press a card to turn it, then another. Matching cards stay up, the others turn back. Choose below what counts as a match: how many shapes, which shape, a number, or the answer of a sum.

What makes a match
Look for the math

Every card hides a whole number from 0 to 29, and each pair of cards was dealt the same number. What you see on a card is only one way to look at that number, and the mode decides which features count.

One number, many faces

The number n gives a shape (n mod 12, one of twelve), a colour (n divided by 12, rounded down) and a count (n mod 5, plus 1). So 29 is the sixth shape, the third colour, drawn 5 times. In "Count 1" two cards match when they show the same number of shapes, which is the same remainder mod 5; in "Count 2" the colour must agree as well. The test checks this rule against the applet's own comparison for every pair of numbers in every mode.

Sums and products with the same answer

In the three arithmetic modes the card shows an expression and matches the one whose result is the same, however it was written: 7+5 matches 20−8 and 3×4 and 36÷3. In Addition the hidden number is 3 less than the sum shown. A difference a − b is built from the answer by adding a small b to it; a product splits the answer into two factors (a number that is prime can only be 1 times itself); a quotient multiplies the answer by 1 to 10. The test builds thousands of cards and checks that each really comes to its number.

How many turns?

With ten pairs there is no way to find a pair for certain without luck: each unseen card could be any of the numbers. But with a good memory you need only 10 turns on top of the cards you uncover while searching. The test plays the perfect game (always turning a card and its partner) and clears the board in exactly 10 turns. Because the numbers are dealt with replacement, two different pairs can share a number, and then any two of those four cards match.

Try Count 1, then Shape. Why is the first so much easier? How many different cards are there in each?
